title: Gbps and Mbps: What Your Internet Speed Really Means
h1: Gbps and Mbps — the network speeds behind every ISP promise
description: A 1 Gbps fibre plan does not download files at 1 GB/s. Here is the bit-vs-byte math and the overheads that eat the rest.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against IEEE 802.3 and RFC 793 overhead calculations

hero: 1 Gbps = 125 MB/s of raw payload. After protocol overhead, real download speed lands around 110 MB/s at best.
body: ISPs advertise link capacity in bits per second because the number is 8× larger than the equivalent bytes-per-second. Consumers download in bytes. The 8× factor is the source of every 'my 500 Mbps plan only downloads at 60 MB/s' complaint.

> 1 byte = 8 bits, always
> 1 Mbps = 10⁶ bits/s = 125,000 bytes/s = 122.07 KiB/s
> 1 Gbps = 10⁹ bits/s = 125 MB/s = 119.2 MiB/s
> 10 Gbps = 1.25 GB/s = 1.164 GiB/s

Ethernet frame overhead: 38 B per 1500 B payload = 2.5% loss. IP + TCP headers: 40 B per packet = 2.7% at 1500 B MTU. HTTPS: 2–5% extra for TLS. Real payload throughput on a 1 Gbps LAN: ~940 Mbps = 117 MB/s. On the internet, latency and packet loss can drop this to 30–60 MB/s even on 1 Gbps plans.

DSL: 5–100 Mbps. Cable: 100 Mbps – 1 Gbps. Fibre-to-home: 100 Mbps – 10 Gbps. WiFi 6: up to ~1 Gbps real-world. Cellular 5G: 100–500 Mbps typical. Local NVMe SSD: 3–7 GB/s = 24–56 Gbps. USB 3.2 Gen 2: 10 Gbps. Thunderbolt 4: 40 Gbps.
## Worked example — downloading a 10 GB game

10 GB game (10¹⁰ bytes) on a 500 Mbps plan. 500 Mbps = 62.5 MB/s theoretical. Realistic sustained: 55 MB/s. Time: 10,000 / 55 = 182 s = 3 minutes. On a 100 Mbps plan: 900 s = 15 minutes. On a 1 Gbps plan: 91 s. Diminishing returns above 500 Mbps for most single-flow downloads because the game server tops out first.

Cable and DSL are asymmetric — download much faster than upload. FTTH is often symmetric (1 Gbps up and down). Consumer expectations of upload speed have risen sharply since videoconferencing became universal; asymmetric plans with 10 Mbps upload are now visibly bottlenecked in real use.
Divide Mbps by 8 for MB/s. Real throughput is 90–95% of advertised on a clean link. Latency and packet loss can drop it much further.

faqs.q: Is 1 Gbps enough for a family of 4?
faqs.a: More than enough. Even 4K Netflix streams at 25 Mbps; a family of 4 streaming simultaneously uses 100 Mbps peak. 1 Gbps is future-proofing.

faqs.q: Why is my WiFi slower than my ISP plan?
faqs.a: WiFi has its own overhead. A '1200 Mbps' WiFi 6 router typically delivers 500–700 Mbps real throughput. Distance, walls and interference reduce this further.

faqs.q: What is 'up to' in ISP marketing?
faqs.a: The peak line rate under ideal conditions. Regulatory bodies (FCC, Ofcom) increasingly require published median speeds instead.
